text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to the Health Report with me, Norman
Swan. Today, putting sleeping in the bank, does it work? The implications of
underestimating caffeine. Foretelling the future through a baby's lungs. Your
genes and your lungs. And the value of seeing your own GP rather than just any
old partner in the practice when you turn up.

Each year an astounding 2.4 million bed days in Australian hospitals could be
avoided. That's over 600,000 admissions to both public and private hospitals and
that's probably an underestimate. At about $5,000 in admission that's a huge
amount of money, not to mention the impact on the people admitted and their
families.

A British study has found that hospital admissions are reduced when people who
have the kind of conditions that can result in an avoidable hospital admission
regularly see the same general practitioner. But there are barriers to this, not
least being the way we pay GPs. Elizabeth Oliver is a general practitioner who
was moved to blog on what patients get for a standard consultation fee of just
over $37. And as you hear her speak to the Health Report's Cathy Johnson, think
back to the last time you've paid for the plumber or electrician who came to your
house or apartment.

Cathy Johnson: So was there something that sent you off, that got you really
mad and made you write this?

Elizabeth Oliver: It actually was the building contractor. I'd spent a standard
consultation looking after him and doing some preventative care and talking
about prostate cancer and bowel cancer had had done this really good job of
setting him up for the next 10 years of his life in terms of his health. And he said
as he walked out, 'Oh, that was easy money for you, wasn't it.' And I kind of
laughed but it just made me think, you've got no idea what good care you just
received and how long it took me to be able to be good enough to give that care
and how much money that took, and that that's in jeopardy.

Cathy Johnson: So you've written this blog, What I Do for $37.05, and the
government's extended freeze on GP pay rates. What's the point that you're
trying to get across?
 
Elizabeth Oliver: The point is that GPs are amazing value for money. I guess I
don't know of any other profession that would accept an eight-year freeze on an
increase in their pay. And so GPs are doing amazing work to save the healthcare
system money and to save people, and that work has been undervalued, and the
more that it's undervalued, the more that GPs get squeezed, the less time they
are going to be able to spend with people and healthcare is going to suffer as a
result. And so is the budget. This isn't just about people's care, it's also about
what we can afford. We must keep people out of hospital, we must stop people's
chronic disease falling apart, we must prevent people going into psychosis. And
these are some of the things that GPs do on a daily basis, and we do that in a
very short amount of time. We are very efficient. And I think that maybe people
don't understand that this is what you get for $37.05. It's not just a complaint, it's
also isn't this awesome. And we're not going to keep doing it for this kind of pay.

Cathy Johnson: What is it about a typical day that makes you so mad about that
mismatch between your reimbursement and what you do?

Elizabeth Oliver: We see everything across the lifespan. We see sick babies, we
see mums who are struggling with postnatal depression and don't know if that's
okay, and we see teenagers who are kind of dabbling with drugs and with mental
health problems, and we see old people who have seven chronic diseases and
that needs to be managed to keep them out of hospital. There is public health
stuff as well. We see people that are going overseas and might bring back
hepatitis A and put it into our food system. We do so many things that not only
increases people's quality of life but saves so much money, and I think that that's
really valuable.

Cathy Johnson: You've mentioned keeping people out of hospital. Is that
something that you feel like you often do?

Elizabeth Oliver: Often. Sometimes I send a patient to hospital because I've
gotten to the point where I can't manage them safely out of hospital anymore,
and I feel almost apologetic to the emergency department doctors for sending
that patient hospital, but they have to go. But then on the back of the mind I think,
do you know what, there were five others today that I could have sent and I didn't
because I managed it myself. You know, the kid with asthma, kept an eye on
them in the waiting room for an hour and now they are looking a bit better so they
 
can go home. I did that for $37. That could have been seen in an emergency
department and cost hundreds and hundreds of dollars. So yes, I definitely think
that GPs do an incredible job and they could be doing a better job if they had a
bit more time and a bit more money.

Cathy Johnson: So it's really time, you're feeling squeezed for time?

Elizabeth Oliver: Yes, absolutely. Sometimes the problem can be solved in, say,
eight minutes, and that's great. But sometimes it requires much more than that,
and sometimes the patient themselves doesn't even know the scope of the
danger of the problem that they are coming in with. I'm not going to keep doing
this. I'm going to stop doing it if it stays like this. I am the good doctor, I have
patients tell me that I'm a great doctor, but I'm not going to keep doing it for this
amount of pay, and for the drain and the toll that it takes on my life, I can't, I can't
keep bulk billing. And I can't continue to deliver good care in that way either, it's
just not viable. I spent a huge amount of time and effort and tears and blood and
money to become a doctor, and I'm really proud to be one and I know that it's a
fantastic privilege and I love my job. But I physically and mentally can't keep
doing this under these bulk billing arrangements and with this Medicare freeze.
GPs need help.

Norman Swan: General practitioner Elizabeth Oliver talking to Cathy Johnson.

Claire Jackson is professor of general practice at the University of Queensland
and heavily involved in reforms to general practice currently being mooted by the
federal government. Claire is in our Brisbane studio, welcome to the Health
Report Claire.

Claire Jackson: Thank you very much Norman, pleasure to be here.

Norman Swan: I take it you've heard…this is not news to you, what you heard
Elizabeth just talking about?

Claire Jackson: No, I think she has nailed many of the issues that have been
circulating in the lay press and also within the profession for a very long time, not
just here in Australia but internationally. Over the 35 years I've been in general
practice there's been a seismic shift in the complexity of the care that we deliver,
 
and the need to have a lot more community resources, both health and social
care, available for general practitioners to work with.

The business case that we are working under at the moment is 35 years old, and
as it is internationally it needs to change in this country, and the Council of
Australian Governments in April signalled a very big change to the way general
practice is delivered and funded in this country, starting with the Healthcare
Home trials in July 1.

Norman Swan: We'll come to that in a moment. Elizabeth thinks…well, I don't
know if she does think, but she implies that the solution is she goes from $37 to
some other figure that is higher than that, but going to $42, for example, is not
going to solve Elizabeth's problem, probably not even going to $70 solves
Elizabeth's problem. So what is this Healthcare Home and how will it get over this
problem which is that you are charged piece rates for what is needed? This trial
in Britain showed the same GP looking after you, continuity of care when you've
got complex chronic problems keeps you out of hospital.

Claire Jackson: And that's absolutely the experience, not only in the UK but in
the US and here in Australia. So the move is to really try and build that continuity
between a patient and a preferred provider, is the term used in the US and also
here in Australia. The national Health and Hospital Reform Commission in 2009
first signalled this and we are now looking at a different model of care for patients
with complex chronic disease…

Norman Swan: Just to be specific, this is people with heart failure, diabetes with
complications, chronic obstructive lung disease, that sort of thing.

Claire Jackson: Yes, the papers describe it as the 10% of Australians who
require 50% of resources, both in person time and also in healthcare funding.
And at the moment they are the people getting a very raw deal from the system.
The National Health Performance Authority last year said that these sort of
patients are being seen over 20 times in general practice and often are seeing
more than five GPs in a year. And for someone with very complex healthcare
needs as Beth described, that's very dangerous. So trying to look at
strengthening the business model for general practice, providing a lot more
holistic ongoing continuous care is the challenge that has been discussed over
 
the last two years, and the Healthcare Home trials that will start next year will try
and build our understanding of what that might look like, what Australian patients
would like to see in that relationship, what sort of opportunities that offers, and
what sort of checks and balances that would need.

Norman Swan: So this is where you would voluntarily…as in the UK where you
register with a GP, in the Healthcare Home you would voluntarily register with a
GP of your choice.

Claire Jackson: So 65,000 Australians in 200 practices across the year will be
invited to participate in this new model of care. It will be entirely voluntary. Only
for patients with really complex chronic conditions. They will enrol in the practice,
which means the practice will offer them a nominated clinician. One would
imagine that would be their general practitioner who was aware of their problems
and priorities and wishes and is responsible for all the coordination of their care
within the practice team but also more generally within the hospital and wider
team. Patients will have access to that clinician and their team, not just face-to-
face which is the way the Medicare rebate recognises it now, but via email,
potentially via videoconference, via phone. That's based around agreements
reached between the patient and their family and the practice. And the hope is
that patients and their family and carers will become much more partners in their
care, that they will build a lot more self-management skills, that they will manage
their own health and be supported in a variety of ways to really build their
confidence about managing their healthcare themselves.

Norman Swan: So how is it going to solve Beth Oliver's problem? Is she going to
get more pay out of it?

Claire Jackson: So the funding model will change to support that. So instead of
Beth needing to see someone sitting beside her in her practice to actually receive
remuneration and for the patient to receive a Medicare rebate, the practice and
practitioner will receive a monthly what is called a bundled payment, to recognise
the costs to that practice of extending that support to patients outside face-to-
face. That is going to be really the focus of the trial, looking at how non-face-to-
face care can really offer benefits to patients and their families and be managed
within the practice in a contemporary manner. We use online banking, we use
online shopping, but unfortunately our Medicare rebates are limited to a face-to-
 
face encounter. This will open that up to what is hoped a lot of innovation
between patients and their practices around how they can best meet the needs
they have outside that face-to-face encounter, which Beth is describing.

Norman Swan: Claire, thanks for joining us.

Claire Jackson: Thank you very much for having me Norman, always a
pleasure.

Norman Swan: Claire Jackson is professor of general practice at the University
of Queensland.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC
Radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

The lung function of a young baby can predict the persistence of asthma in
young adults. And kids who develop asthma, their lung function soon after birth
can help to find out those whose asthma will resolve before adulthood. This is all
according to pioneering Western Australian research which has now been going
on for nearly 25 years, and may tell us a lot about the importance of pregnancy
for lung development. The Health Report covered this study in its early days and
now they are reporting on the babies who have grown up to be grown-ups. To tell
us more is the lead author and paediatric respiratory physician Louisa Owens.
Thanks for joining us Louisa.

Louisa Owens: Thanks for having me Norman.

Norman Swan: When you talk about infant lung function, what are we actually
talking about here?

Louisa Owens: Well, there's a number of different tests that you can do in
infancy, and for a small babies, and these have evolved over the last number of
years. So actually the tests that we did back in the late '80s in this study have
changed quite considerably or evolved I guess to what we do now. But we are
trying to mimic the lung function tests that older children and adults can do, so it's
something that we can follow longitudinally to see how it changes with time.

Norman Swan: So mimicking how much you can blow out in a second, that sort
of thing.
 
Louisa Owens: Exactly yes. So with small babies we have to sedate them so
that they are asleep, because we need to measure their breathing while they are
relaxed. And we use different manoeuvres. So we can put a jacket around their
chest which we put a balloon inside it and inflate the balloon and that causes
them to breathe out forcefully and we measure that flow. We can also get them to
breathe a gas and see how long it takes them to breathe the gas out to see how
much blockage there is in the airways.

Norman Swan: So once you've measured that…and at what age?

Louisa Owens: So we can do it from birth. It's been done even in preterm
infants, but really from about two months of age they need to be sedated, before
that you can do it just in gentle sleep.

Norman Swan: So the findings that you've made have been related to babies
that have reduced lung function at birth and then following them through?

Louisa Owens: Exactly. So this was based on the Perth Infant Asthma Follow-
up study which was initiated by Professors Lou Landau and Peter Le Souëf. And
they initially recruited a normal cohort from an antenatal hospital in Perth. So
mothers who were pregnant were recruited onto this study, and their infants were
then tested during infancy, their lung function was tested and they have been
followed up, they are now 24 to 26 years old and we are still looking at their lung
function to see how it has evolved right throughout childhood and adolescence.

Norman Swan: So tell me what you found in the 25-year-olds or the 24-year-
olds?

Louisa Owens: When we were specifically looking at those who had asthma, so
the 24-year-olds, the young adults who had asthma, we were able to look back
and see that their lung function had been significantly lower in infancy, just one
month of age. So shortly after birth their lung function was already reduced,
suggesting that their asthma was really due to in utero development.

Norman Swan: So they had smaller airways?

Louisa Owens: Smaller airways, yes, which can be related to the size of the
infant. So we corrected for the size of the infant and found that they had smaller
 
airways and lower flow. I guess they were breathing out slower, than those who
didn't have asthma at 24 years of age. And it was a very significant difference
that we could see.

Norman Swan: Presumably there was variation amongst that, it wasn't one and
one, but it just increased the risk of having asthma as an adult when you tended
to have low infant lung function.

Louisa Owens: Absolutely. And one of the limitations of the infant lung function
testing is that there is quite a wide variability. But when we looked back, there
was only 13% of those with asthma at 24 who had normal lung function in
infancy, so it was a significantly smaller number who had lower lung function.

Norman Swan: And when they developed asthma in childhood and they had
relatively normal lung function in infancy, they tended to grow out of the asthma,
predicted them growing out of the asthma.

Louisa Owens: Exactly, yes. So those who had asthma during childhood but no
symptoms in early adulthood, they had normal lung function in infancy when we
looked back.

Norman Swan: In the paper you've linked this to a smoking-related disease
which is what we were talking about with Claire and Elizabeth Oliver a moment
ago which is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease which is one of the chronic
diseases that GPs look after and people end up in hospital. What's the link here,
do you think, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

Louisa Owens: Well, we've known that adults with asthma have lower lung
function, and it was initially thought to be related to chronic inflammation and
recurrent exacerbations of their asthma but now we are finding we can link that
right back to infancy, so it's more likely that it's related to in utero development.
So the next step of our study is to specifically look at both in utero smoke
exposure, postnatal smoke exposure, and also the genes that affect it, because it
appears as though some babies are more vulnerable to the toxic effects of in
utero smoke exposure, so possibly a gene environment interaction. So we'd be
looking at that.
 
Norman Swan: But when I interviewed Lou Landau about this probably 20-odd
years ago, he said it was definitely linked to smoking, but you think it's not?
Some mothers who don't smoke do have babies with reduced infant lung
function, is that what you're saying?

Louisa Owens: So we've certainly shown that smoking is related to reduced lung
function in infancy, but we haven't yet shown that that then links to asthma later
on. So that's what we'll been looking at separately. But also following the lung
function to see those who do or don't have asthma, how their lung function right
throughout childhood and adolescence is affected by smoking…

Norman Swan: So just briefly, because we are running out of time, apart from
not smoking there is nothing you know yet to tell parents or mothers to optimise
the lung function of their babies at birth?

Louisa Owens: No, we haven't been able to target specifically what it is that
causes the low lung function. Certainly in utero smoke exposure has toxic
effects. So we need to look a little bit closer at that to figure out first of all what
specifically in the child makes them more vulnerable to tobacco smoke, and if
there is something we can do to target that.

Norman Swan: Louisa, thank you.

Louisa Owens: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Louisa Owens is a respiratory physician who's now at the
Sydney Children's Hospital.

And we'll move on to genes now, a very relevant follow-through, what might be
important related findings. A huge international project which involved a study of
people living in the Busselton area of Western Australia has identified 43 new
genetic signals that might indicate a person is up to 3.7 times more likely to be at
risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. That brings the total of known
genetic signals to nearly 100. Professor Alan James is a respiratory physician at
Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital in Perth and one of the enormous team involved.
Thank you for making time with us, Alan.

Alan James: Nice to be here Norman.
 
Norman Swan: So are these the genes that Louisa was just talking about, that
give you an infant with small lungs?

Alan James: Yes, the first line in the paper that we're talking about states that
maximally attained lung function and subsequent decline all contribute to the risk
of developing COPD. And so we know that events throughout life contribute to
what our lung function is later in life, and certainly I'd agree that in utero
development may be a contributing factor to not attaining full lung function.

Norman Swan: The study has got a mindbending name called the Genome
Wide Association Study, GWAS. And these are like sort of fishing exercises
where you go out hunting and fishing for genes in populations where you know
they've got respiratory problems or don't. Is that a reasonable description, if
somewhat pejorative?

Alan James: Some people put it in a pejorative way and others…

Norman Swan: Stamp collecting is what some people call it, yes.

Alan James: And others look upon it more optimistically. We know from looking
at populations like Busselton and other population studies of lung function, that
by studying family members and unrelated members, that about 40% of lung
function is probably related to inherited factors, including genes and epigenetic
effects.

Norman Swan: And just hold on a second, epigenetic effects are where the gene
itself is not mutated but something happens around the outside to change its
shape and the way it interacts with proteins and so on. Literally what it means is
an 'on the outside' phenomenon rather than on the inside with DNA.

Alan James: Right, something that can determine whether the gene is turned off
or on, that arises in the environment, but then is inherited by offspring. So 40% of
these effects seen to be important in determining our lung function. And what this
large fishing expedition has shown, we've uncovered up to about 10% of those
genes now using these very large studies of sites on the genome that are likely
to be affecting lung function.
 
Norman Swan: And so coming back to the conversation with Louisa, are these
genes that interact with smoking or are they genes that knacker your lungs no
matter what?

Alan James: Well, interestingly only one gene of the 43 new genes or new sites
that were discovered seems to be related to smoking. Most of the signals that
were related to identify genes seem to be related to inflammation, lung structure
and smooth muscle, all of which affect airway and lung function. So not much
related to smoking.

Norman Swan: Is it related to asthma?

Alan James: And these may be relevant to asthma of course, which is related
again to your lung function.

Norman Swan: Again, we don't have a lot of time, but one of the problems with
genome-wide association studies is that each individual genetic signal is often
incredibly rare. To what extent are you…you know, somebody is listening,
they've got asthma or chronic lung disease, are these genes relevant to them?

Alan James: Well, this is what we are finding more and more, this is why we
have to look at large numbers because it's probable that the genetic effect of lung
function may vary from family to family, so families are unalike and that not just
one single gene or a few handfuls of genes determines lung function across a
whole population.

Norman Swan: But you think you've found genes that might be potential drug
targets?

Alan James: Yes, there was two or three genes related to what we call the
acetylcholine receptor. Acetylcholine is a chemical that determines neural
function and its transmission to muscle. And there are already drugs that we are
using to treat asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease, and it may be that
finding genes like this can help us identify people who are going to benefit most
from those sorts of treatments and provide goals for new treatments.

Norman Swan: Alan, thanks for joining us.

Alan James: It's a pleasure Norman.
 
Norman Swan: Professor Alan James is a respiratory physician at Sir Charles
Gairdner Hospital in Perth.

And you're listening to the Health Report, which indeed is coming today from
Perth.

Let's leave the lungs for our sleep and jetlag because WA steadfastly clings to
the belief that daylight saving fades the curtains, there's a three-our gap with the
east, apart from Queensland where they still believe that daylight saving fades
the curtains. So I am coming to you at nearly 3pm western time. Ian Dunican of
UWA's Centre for Sleep Science is studying sleep and jetlag, and his subjects
are the Western Force, WA's super rugby franchise who have to travel a lot for
their fixtures. Welcome to the Health Report, Ian. So is there a problem with
Western Force?

Ian Dunican: Well, there's not such a problem with Western Force, but they do
provide a unique opportunity for us to investigate the effect of jetlag on
performance, cognitive and physical, within the super rugby competition.

Norman Swan: So they are flying all over the place, it's not just the three-hour
lag to the east.

Ian Dunican: For sure, they are the most travelled sports team in the world, they
travel to South Africa, Japan, New Zealand, to the east coast of Australia, and
now in this year they will be travelling to Argentina for the first time ever.

Norman Swan: So how are you studying them?

Ian Dunican: So we are using a range of different methods over the past few
years with the Western Force, but more specifically this year we are using
biomathematical modelling which allows us to determine the cognitive
performance effectiveness of the players individually and at a team level, and this
is done by a range of different factors, including the use of wrist activity monitors
from a company called Fatigue Science.

Norman Swan: And what are you finding?

Ian Dunican: Well, we are finding that on average athletes are sleeping just a
little bit short of seven hours a night, which is not optimal, and indeed recent…
 
Norman Swan: More than I get! Probably more than you get too.

Ian Dunican: Indeed, recent Sleep Health Foundation statistics show that adults
are getting around seven hours, so athletes are no different.

Norman Swan: You're also finding that they are sleep banking, in other words
they are sleeping more before matches, which is what people say you shouldn't
do, there is no advantage to banking up your sleep.

Ian Dunican: Well, in the general population we do try to encourage people to
have a routine around sleep, but for professional athletes it's not so easy, with
travel, training and so on. So athletes on the night before the game in this
environment seem to tend to bank sleep or optimise sleep the night before to get
through those periods.

Norman Swan: And does that improve their cognitive score?

Ian Dunican: It does, it drives up the cognitive score for before the game and
during the game.

Norman Swan: Because cognitive scores…I think one of your statistics is that
77%, it's the same as having a .05 level of alcohol in your blood.

Ian Dunican: Indeed, and that can equate as well to an increase in reaction time
by 34%, so basically they are getting worse.

Norman Swan: And the use of caffeine?

Ian Dunican: Yes, so caffeine has been widely used across…

Norman Swan: And that's legal?

Ian Dunican: It is legal, yes.

Norman Swan: And what's that doing to them? Screwing them up or giving them
better performance or what?

Ian Dunican: So, many athletes take caffeine for ergogenic performance for
during the game…
 
Norman Swan: So to generate energy.

Ian Dunican: Yes. But the negative effect is post-game from the timing of the
caffeine affects the time of sleep onset. So in a general population we see the
same thing. Caffeine full-life and half-life, the caffeine half-life being between four
and six hours can actually stop people falling asleep.

Norman Swan: So you've re-timed when they take their caffeine for the benefit
during the match.

Ian Dunican: Yes, for sure.

Norman Swan: So what have you learnt? If it works for athletes, sleep banking
for example, surely it's going to work for us. So what have you learnt for the
common or garden non-rugby player here?

Ian Dunican: So we see sleep banking or sleep optimisation being utilised in
other areas as well, such as military. But for people who may not be getting
sufficient sleep, such as shift workers, particularly here in Western Australia in
the mining, oil and gas industry, sleep banking or sleep optimisation can indeed
help for recovery after periods of sleep loss. Ideally the general routine and sleep
hygiene is the best way to go, but if you do know you're going to come up to
periods of sleep loss, sleep banking can indeed help people to override those
negative cognitive effects.

Norman Swan: So adolescent males know something here.

Ian Dunican: Well, more recently we've found with elite athletes at the AIS that
young athletes and teenagers have a delayed chronotype, so they like to go to
bed later and sleep in. So that's just their normal circadian physiology, so they
have an evening chronotype.

Norman Swan: And caffeine…well, we kind of know that already, earlier in the
day rather than later.

Ian Dunican: Yes, for sure. We see this in the general population and with
athletes. We tend to advise athletes not to have caffeine habitually after 2 o'clock
in the afternoon, same with the general population. And even before matches if
 
we can avoid caffeine for 24 to 48 hours we can get a better ergogenic effect
from the caffeine prior to the game.

Norman Swan: So if you deposit some sleep in the bank, don't remove it with
some caffeine.

Ian Dunican: Exactly.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much Ian Dunican, who is at the University of
Western Australia's Centre for Sleep Science.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, see you next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to the Health Report with me, Norman
Swan. Today, putting sleeping in the bank, does it work? The implications of
underestimating caffeine. Foretelling the future through a baby's lungs. Your
genes and your lungs. And the value of seeing your own GP rather than just any
old partner in the practice when you turn up.

Each year an astounding 2.4 million bed days in Australian hospitals could be
avoided. That's over 600,000 admissions to both public and private hospitals and
that's probably an underestimate. At about $5,000 in admission that's a huge
amount of money, not to mention the impact on the people admitted and their
families.

A British study has found that hospital admissions are reduced when people who
have the kind of conditions that can result in an avoidable hospital admission
regularly see the same general practitioner. But there are barriers to this, not
least being the way we pay GPs. Elizabeth Oliver is a general practitioner who
was moved to blog on what patients get for a standard consultation fee of just
over $37. And as you hear her speak to the Health Report's Cathy Johnson, think
back to the last time you've paid for the plumber or electrician who came to your
house or apartment.

Cathy Johnson: So was there something that sent you off, that got you really
mad and made you write this?

Elizabeth Oliver: It actually was the building contractor. I'd spent a standard
consultation looking after him and doing some preventative care and talking
about prostate cancer and bowel cancer had had done this really good job of
setting him up for the next 10 years of his life in terms of his health. And he said
as he walked out, 'Oh, that was easy money for you, wasn't it.' And I kind of
laughed but it just made me think, you've got no idea what good care you just
received and how long it took me to be able to be good enough to give that care
and how much money that took, and that that's in jeopardy.

Cathy Johnson: So you've written this blog, What I Do for $37.05, and the
government's extended freeze on GP pay rates. What's the point that you're
trying to get across?

Elizabeth Oliver: The point is that GPs are amazing value for money. I guess I
don't know of any other profession that would accept an eight-year freeze on an
increase in their pay. And so GPs are doing amazing work to save the healthcare
system money and to save people, and that work has been undervalued, and the
more that it's undervalued, the more that GPs get squeezed, the less time they
are going to be able to spend with people and healthcare is going to suffer as a
result. And so is the budget. This isn't just about people's care, it's also about
what we can afford. We must keep people out of hospital, we must stop people's
chronic disease falling apart, we must prevent people going into psychosis. And
these are some of the things that GPs do on a daily basis, and we do that in a
very short amount of time. We are very efficient. And I think that maybe people
don't understand that this is what you get for $37.05. It's not just a complaint, it's
also isn't this awesome. And we're not going to keep doing it for this kind of pay.

Cathy Johnson: What is it about a typical day that makes you so mad about that
mismatch between your reimbursement and what you do?

Elizabeth Oliver: We see everything across the lifespan. We see sick babies, we
see mums who are struggling with postnatal depression and don't know if that's
okay, and we see teenagers who are kind of dabbling with drugs and with mental
health problems, and we see old people who have seven chronic diseases and
that needs to be managed to keep them out of hospital. There is public health
stuff as well. We see people that are going overseas and might bring back
hepatitis A and put it into our food system. We do so many things that not only
increases people's quality of life but saves so much money, and I think that that's
really valuable.

Cathy Johnson: You've mentioned keeping people out of hospital. Is that
something that you feel like you often do?

Elizabeth Oliver: Often. Sometimes I send a patient to hospital because I've
gotten to the point where I can't manage them safely out of hospital anymore,
and I feel almost apologetic to the emergency department doctors for sending
that patient hospital, but they have to go. But then on the back of the mind I think,
do you know what, there were five others today that I could have sent and I didn't
because I managed it myself. You know, the kid with asthma, kept an eye on
them in the waiting room for an hour and now they are looking a bit better so they

can go home. I did that for $37. That could have been seen in an emergency
department and cost hundreds and hundreds of dollars. So yes, I definitely think
that GPs do an incredible job and they could be doing a better job if they had a
bit more time and a bit more money.

Cathy Johnson: So it's really time, you're feeling squeezed for time?

Elizabeth Oliver: Yes, absolutely. Sometimes the problem can be solved in, say,
eight minutes, and that's great. But sometimes it requires much more than that,
and sometimes the patient themselves doesn't even know the scope of the
danger of the problem that they are coming in with. I'm not going to keep doing
this. I'm going to stop doing it if it stays like this. I am the good doctor, I have
patients tell me that I'm a great doctor, but I'm not going to keep doing it for this
amount of pay, and for the drain and the toll that it takes on my life, I can't, I can't
keep bulk billing. And I can't continue to deliver good care in that way either, it's
just not viable. I spent a huge amount of time and effort and tears and blood and
money to become a doctor, and I'm really proud to be one and I know that it's a
fantastic privilege and I love my job. But I physically and mentally can't keep
doing this under these bulk billing arrangements and with this Medicare freeze.
GPs need help.

Norman Swan: General practitioner Elizabeth Oliver talking to Cathy Johnson.

Claire Jackson is professor of general practice at the University of Queensland
and heavily involved in reforms to general practice currently being mooted by the
federal government. Claire is in our Brisbane studio, welcome to the Health
Report Claire.

Claire Jackson: Thank you very much Norman, pleasure to be here.

Norman Swan: I take it you've heard…this is not news to you, what you heard
Elizabeth just talking about?

Claire Jackson: No, I think she has nailed many of the issues that have been
circulating in the lay press and also within the profession for a very long time, not
just here in Australia but internationally. Over the 35 years I've been in general
practice there's been a seismic shift in the complexity of the care that we deliver,

and the need to have a lot more community resources, both health and social
care, available for general practitioners to work with.

The business case that we are working under at the moment is 35 years old, and
as it is internationally it needs to change in this country, and the Council of
Australian Governments in April signalled a very big change to the way general
practice is delivered and funded in this country, starting with the Healthcare
Home trials in July 1.

Norman Swan: We'll come to that in a moment. Elizabeth thinks…well, I don't
know if she does think, but she implies that the solution is she goes from $37 to
some other figure that is higher than that, but going to $42, for example, is not
going to solve Elizabeth's problem, probably not even going to $70 solves
Elizabeth's problem. So what is this Healthcare Home and how will it get over this
problem which is that you are charged piece rates for what is needed? This trial
in Britain showed the same GP looking after you, continuity of care when you've
got complex chronic problems keeps you out of hospital.

Claire Jackson: And that's absolutely the experience, not only in the UK but in
the US and here in Australia. So the move is to really try and build that continuity
between a patient and a preferred provider, is the term used in the US and also
here in Australia. The national Health and Hospital Reform Commission in 2009
first signalled this and we are now looking at a different model of care for patients
with complex chronic disease…

Norman Swan: Just to be specific, this is people with heart failure, diabetes with
complications, chronic obstructive lung disease, that sort of thing.

Claire Jackson: Yes, the papers describe it as the 10% of Australians who
require 50% of resources, both in person time and also in healthcare funding.
And at the moment they are the people getting a very raw deal from the system.
The National Health Performance Authority last year said that these sort of
patients are being seen over 20 times in general practice and often are seeing
more than five GPs in a year. And for someone with very complex healthcare
needs as Beth described, that's very dangerous. So trying to look at
strengthening the business model for general practice, providing a lot more
holistic ongoing continuous care is the challenge that has been discussed over

the last two years, and the Healthcare Home trials that will start next year will try
and build our understanding of what that might look like, what Australian patients
would like to see in that relationship, what sort of opportunities that offers, and
what sort of checks and balances that would need.

Norman Swan: So this is where you would voluntarily…as in the UK where you
register with a GP, in the Healthcare Home you would voluntarily register with a
GP of your choice.

Claire Jackson: So 65,000 Australians in 200 practices across the year will be
invited to participate in this new model of care. It will be entirely voluntary. Only
for patients with really complex chronic conditions. They will enrol in the practice,
which means the practice will offer them a nominated clinician. One would
imagine that would be their general practitioner who was aware of their problems
and priorities and wishes and is responsible for all the coordination of their care
within the practice team but also more generally within the hospital and wider
team. Patients will have access to that clinician and their team, not just face-to-
face which is the way the Medicare rebate recognises it now, but via email,
potentially via videoconference, via phone. That's based around agreements
reached between the patient and their family and the practice. And the hope is
that patients and their family and carers will become much more partners in their
care, that they will build a lot more self-management skills, that they will manage
their own health and be supported in a variety of ways to really build their
confidence about managing their healthcare themselves.

Norman Swan: So how is it going to solve Beth Oliver's problem? Is she going to
get more pay out of it?

Claire Jackson: So the funding model will change to support that. So instead of
Beth needing to see someone sitting beside her in her practice to actually receive
remuneration and for the patient to receive a Medicare rebate, the practice and
practitioner will receive a monthly what is called a bundled payment, to recognise
the costs to that practice of extending that support to patients outside face-to-
face. That is going to be really the focus of the trial, looking at how non-face-to-
face care can really offer benefits to patients and their families and be managed
within the practice in a contemporary manner. We use online banking, we use
online shopping, but unfortunately our Medicare rebates are limited to a face-to-

face encounter. This will open that up to what is hoped a lot of innovation
between patients and their practices around how they can best meet the needs
they have outside that face-to-face encounter, which Beth is describing.

Norman Swan: Claire, thanks for joining us.

Claire Jackson: Thank you very much for having me Norman, always a
pleasure.

Norman Swan: Claire Jackson is professor of general practice at the University
of Queensland.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC
Radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

The lung function of a young baby can predict the persistence of asthma in
young adults. And kids who develop asthma, their lung function soon after birth
can help to find out those whose asthma will resolve before adulthood. This is all
according to pioneering Western Australian research which has now been going
on for nearly 25 years, and may tell us a lot about the importance of pregnancy
for lung development. The Health Report covered this study in its early days and
now they are reporting on the babies who have grown up to be grown-ups. To tell
us more is the lead author and paediatric respiratory physician Louisa Owens.
Thanks for joining us Louisa.

Louisa Owens: Thanks for having me Norman.

Norman Swan: When you talk about infant lung function, what are we actually
talking about here?

Louisa Owens: Well, there's a number of different tests that you can do in
infancy, and for a small babies, and these have evolved over the last number of
years. So actually the tests that we did back in the late '80s in this study have
changed quite considerably or evolved I guess to what we do now. But we are
trying to mimic the lung function tests that older children and adults can do, so it's
something that we can follow longitudinally to see how it changes with time.

Norman Swan: So mimicking how much you can blow out in a second, that sort
of thing.

Louisa Owens: Exactly yes. So with small babies we have to sedate them so
that they are asleep, because we need to measure their breathing while they are
relaxed. And we use different manoeuvres. So we can put a jacket around their
chest which we put a balloon inside it and inflate the balloon and that causes
them to breathe out forcefully and we measure that flow. We can also get them to
breathe a gas and see how long it takes them to breathe the gas out to see how
much blockage there is in the airways.

Norman Swan: So once you've measured that…and at what age?

Louisa Owens: So we can do it from birth. It's been done even in preterm
infants, but really from about two months of age they need to be sedated, before
that you can do it just in gentle sleep.

Norman Swan: So the findings that you've made have been related to babies
that have reduced lung function at birth and then following them through?

Louisa Owens: Exactly. So this was based on the Perth Infant Asthma Follow-
up study which was initiated by Professors Lou Landau and Peter Le Souëf. And
they initially recruited a normal cohort from an antenatal hospital in Perth. So
mothers who were pregnant were recruited onto this study, and their infants were
then tested during infancy, their lung function was tested and they have been
followed up, they are now 24 to 26 years old and we are still looking at their lung
function to see how it has evolved right throughout childhood and adolescence.

Norman Swan: So tell me what you found in the 25-year-olds or the 24-year-
olds?

Louisa Owens: When we were specifically looking at those who had asthma, so
the 24-year-olds, the young adults who had asthma, we were able to look back
and see that their lung function had been significantly lower in infancy, just one
month of age. So shortly after birth their lung function was already reduced,
suggesting that their asthma was really due to in utero development.

Norman Swan: So they had smaller airways?

Louisa Owens: Smaller airways, yes, which can be related to the size of the
infant. So we corrected for the size of the infant and found that they had smaller

airways and lower flow. I guess they were breathing out slower, than those who
didn't have asthma at 24 years of age. And it was a very significant difference
that we could see.

Norman Swan: Presumably there was variation amongst that, it wasn't one and
one, but it just increased the risk of having asthma as an adult when you tended
to have low infant lung function.

Louisa Owens: Absolutely. And one of the limitations of the infant lung function
testing is that there is quite a wide variability. But when we looked back, there
was only 13% of those with asthma at 24 who had normal lung function in
infancy, so it was a significantly smaller number who had lower lung function.

Norman Swan: And when they developed asthma in childhood and they had
relatively normal lung function in infancy, they tended to grow out of the asthma,
predicted them growing out of the asthma.

Louisa Owens: Exactly, yes. So those who had asthma during childhood but no
symptoms in early adulthood, they had normal lung function in infancy when we
looked back.

Norman Swan: In the paper you've linked this to a smoking-related disease
which is what we were talking about with Claire and Elizabeth Oliver a moment
ago which is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease which is one of the chronic
diseases that GPs look after and people end up in hospital. What's the link here,
do you think, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

Louisa Owens: Well, we've known that adults with asthma have lower lung
function, and it was initially thought to be related to chronic inflammation and
recurrent exacerbations of their asthma but now we are finding we can link that
right back to infancy, so it's more likely that it's related to in utero development.
So the next step of our study is to specifically look at both in utero smoke
exposure, postnatal smoke exposure, and also the genes that affect it, because it
appears as though some babies are more vulnerable to the toxic effects of in
utero smoke exposure, so possibly a gene environment interaction. So we'd be
looking at that.

Norman Swan: But when I interviewed Lou Landau about this probably 20-odd
years ago, he said it was definitely linked to smoking, but you think it's not?
Some mothers who don't smoke do have babies with reduced infant lung
function, is that what you're saying?

Louisa Owens: So we've certainly shown that smoking is related to reduced lung
function in infancy, but we haven't yet shown that that then links to asthma later
on. So that's what we'll been looking at separately. But also following the lung
function to see those who do or don't have asthma, how their lung function right
throughout childhood and adolescence is affected by smoking…

Norman Swan: So just briefly, because we are running out of time, apart from
not smoking there is nothing you know yet to tell parents or mothers to optimise
the lung function of their babies at birth?

Louisa Owens: No, we haven't been able to target specifically what it is that
causes the low lung function. Certainly in utero smoke exposure has toxic
effects. So we need to look a little bit closer at that to figure out first of all what
specifically in the child makes them more vulnerable to tobacco smoke, and if
there is something we can do to target that.

Norman Swan: Louisa, thank you.

Louisa Owens: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Louisa Owens is a respiratory physician who's now at the
Sydney Children's Hospital.

And we'll move on to genes now, a very relevant follow-through, what might be
important related findings. A huge international project which involved a study of
people living in the Busselton area of Western Australia has identified 43 new
genetic signals that might indicate a person is up to 3.7 times more likely to be at
risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. That brings the total of known
genetic signals to nearly 100. Professor Alan James is a respiratory physician at
Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital in Perth and one of the enormous team involved.
Thank you for making time with us, Alan.

Alan James: Nice to be here Norman.

Norman Swan: So are these the genes that Louisa was just talking about, that
give you an infant with small lungs?

Alan James: Yes, the first line in the paper that we're talking about states that
maximally attained lung function and subsequent decline all contribute to the risk
of developing COPD. And so we know that events throughout life contribute to
what our lung function is later in life, and certainly I'd agree that in utero
development may be a contributing factor to not attaining full lung function.

Norman Swan: The study has got a mindbending name called the Genome
Wide Association Study, GWAS. And these are like sort of fishing exercises
where you go out hunting and fishing for genes in populations where you know
they've got respiratory problems or don't. Is that a reasonable description, if
somewhat pejorative?

Alan James: Some people put it in a pejorative way and others…

Norman Swan: Stamp collecting is what some people call it, yes.

Alan James: And others look upon it more optimistically. We know from looking
at populations like Busselton and other population studies of lung function, that
by studying family members and unrelated members, that about 40% of lung
function is probably related to inherited factors, including genes and epigenetic
effects.

Norman Swan: And just hold on a second, epigenetic effects are where the gene
itself is not mutated but something happens around the outside to change its
shape and the way it interacts with proteins and so on. Literally what it means is
an 'on the outside' phenomenon rather than on the inside with DNA.

Alan James: Right, something that can determine whether the gene is turned off
or on, that arises in the environment, but then is inherited by offspring. So 40% of
these effects seen to be important in determining our lung function. And what this
large fishing expedition has shown, we've uncovered up to about 10% of those
genes now using these very large studies of sites on the genome that are likely
to be affecting lung function.

Norman Swan: And so coming back to the conversation with Louisa, are these
genes that interact with smoking or are they genes that knacker your lungs no
matter what?

Alan James: Well, interestingly only one gene of the 43 new genes or new sites
that were discovered seems to be related to smoking. Most of the signals that
were related to identify genes seem to be related to inflammation, lung structure
and smooth muscle, all of which affect airway and lung function. So not much
related to smoking.

Norman Swan: Is it related to asthma?

Alan James: And these may be relevant to asthma of course, which is related
again to your lung function.

Norman Swan: Again, we don't have a lot of time, but one of the problems with
genome-wide association studies is that each individual genetic signal is often
incredibly rare. To what extent are you…you know, somebody is listening,
they've got asthma or chronic lung disease, are these genes relevant to them?

Alan James: Well, this is what we are finding more and more, this is why we
have to look at large numbers because it's probable that the genetic effect of lung
function may vary from family to family, so families are unalike and that not just
one single gene or a few handfuls of genes determines lung function across a
whole population.

Norman Swan: But you think you've found genes that might be potential drug
targets?

Alan James: Yes, there was two or three genes related to what we call the
acetylcholine receptor. Acetylcholine is a chemical that determines neural
function and its transmission to muscle. And there are already drugs that we are
using to treat asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease, and it may be that
finding genes like this can help us identify people who are going to benefit most
from those sorts of treatments and provide goals for new treatments.

Norman Swan: Alan, thanks for joining us.

Alan James: It's a pleasure Norman.

Norman Swan: Professor Alan James is a respiratory physician at Sir Charles
Gairdner Hospital in Perth.

And you're listening to the Health Report, which indeed is coming today from
Perth.

Let's leave the lungs for our sleep and jetlag because WA steadfastly clings to
the belief that daylight saving fades the curtains, there's a three-our gap with the
east, apart from Queensland where they still believe that daylight saving fades
the curtains. So I am coming to you at nearly 3pm western time. Ian Dunican of
UWA's Centre for Sleep Science is studying sleep and jetlag, and his subjects
are the Western Force, WA's super rugby franchise who have to travel a lot for
their fixtures. Welcome to the Health Report, Ian. So is there a problem with
Western Force?

Ian Dunican: Well, there's not such a problem with Western Force, but they do
provide a unique opportunity for us to investigate the effect of jetlag on
performance, cognitive and physical, within the super rugby competition.

Norman Swan: So they are flying all over the place, it's not just the three-hour
lag to the east.

Ian Dunican: For sure, they are the most travelled sports team in the world, they
travel to South Africa, Japan, New Zealand, to the east coast of Australia, and
now in this year they will be travelling to Argentina for the first time ever.

Norman Swan: So how are you studying them?

Ian Dunican: So we are using a range of different methods over the past few
years with the Western Force, but more specifically this year we are using
biomathematical modelling which allows us to determine the cognitive
performance effectiveness of the players individually and at a team level, and this
is done by a range of different factors, including the use of wrist activity monitors
from a company called Fatigue Science.

Norman Swan: And what are you finding?

Ian Dunican: Well, we are finding that on average athletes are sleeping just a
little bit short of seven hours a night, which is not optimal, and indeed recent…

Norman Swan: More than I get! Probably more than you get too.

Ian Dunican: Indeed, recent Sleep Health Foundation statistics show that adults
are getting around seven hours, so athletes are no different.

Norman Swan: You're also finding that they are sleep banking, in other words
they are sleeping more before matches, which is what people say you shouldn't
do, there is no advantage to banking up your sleep.

Ian Dunican: Well, in the general population we do try to encourage people to
have a routine around sleep, but for professional athletes it's not so easy, with
travel, training and so on. So athletes on the night before the game in this
environment seem to tend to bank sleep or optimise sleep the night before to get
through those periods.

Norman Swan: And does that improve their cognitive score?

Ian Dunican: It does, it drives up the cognitive score for before the game and
during the game.

Norman Swan: Because cognitive scores…I think one of your statistics is that
77%, it's the same as having a .05 level of alcohol in your blood.

Ian Dunican: Indeed, and that can equate as well to an increase in reaction time
by 34%, so basically they are getting worse.

Norman Swan: And the use of caffeine?

Ian Dunican: Yes, so caffeine has been widely used across…

Norman Swan: And that's legal?

Ian Dunican: It is legal, yes.

Norman Swan: And what's that doing to them? Screwing them up or giving them
better performance or what?

Ian Dunican: So, many athletes take caffeine for ergogenic performance for
during the game…

Norman Swan: So to generate energy.

Ian Dunican: Yes. But the negative effect is post-game from the timing of the
caffeine affects the time of sleep onset. So in a general population we see the
same thing. Caffeine full-life and half-life, the caffeine half-life being between four
and six hours can actually stop people falling asleep.

Norman Swan: So you've re-timed when they take their caffeine for the benefit
during the match.

Ian Dunican: Yes, for sure.

Norman Swan: So what have you learnt? If it works for athletes, sleep banking
for example, surely it's going to work for us. So what have you learnt for the
common or garden non-rugby player here?

Ian Dunican: So we see sleep banking or sleep optimisation being utilised in
other areas as well, such as military. But for people who may not be getting
sufficient sleep, such as shift workers, particularly here in Western Australia in
the mining, oil and gas industry, sleep banking or sleep optimisation can indeed
help for recovery after periods of sleep loss. Ideally the general routine and sleep
hygiene is the best way to go, but if you do know you're going to come up to
periods of sleep loss, sleep banking can indeed help people to override those
negative cognitive effects.

Norman Swan: So adolescent males know something here.

Ian Dunican: Well, more recently we've found with elite athletes at the AIS that
young athletes and teenagers have a delayed chronotype, so they like to go to
bed later and sleep in. So that's just their normal circadian physiology, so they
have an evening chronotype.

Norman Swan: And caffeine…well, we kind of know that already, earlier in the
day rather than later.

Ian Dunican: Yes, for sure. We see this in the general population and with
athletes. We tend to advise athletes not to have caffeine habitually after 2 o'clock
in the afternoon, same with the general population. And even before matches if

we can avoid caffeine for 24 to 48 hours we can get a better ergogenic effect
from the caffeine prior to the game.

Norman Swan: So if you deposit some sleep in the bank, don't remove it with
some caffeine.

Ian Dunican: Exactly.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much Ian Dunican, who is at the University of
Western Australia's Centre for Sleep Science.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, see you next week.
